content: Black hairy tongue is a condition observed in both humans and animals, characterized by an unusual dark and/or hairy appearance of the tongue. In humans, it is a benign condition caused by fungal growth on the dorsal surface of the tongue. This condition is often associated with elderly individuals and is linked to the use of antibiotics. It is more frequently observed in tobacco smokers. While the most common color associated with this condition is black, other colors such as brown, white, green, or pink may also occur, often influenced by secondary factors like mouthwashes or breath mints. In humans, the condition known as hairy tongue (lingua villosa) arises due to defective desquamation of the filiform papillae, which can result from various precipitating factors. These factors include poor oral hygiene, tooth loss (as a soft diet may not facilitate normal desquamation through mechanical scraping of the tongue by rough foods), chronic or extensive antibiotic use, and radiation treatments to the head and neck. Hairy tongue is more commonly seen in individuals who consume coffee or tea and those who use tobacco. It is also frequently observed in patients who are HIV-positive or use intravenous drugs, although the presence of hairy tongue does not have predictive value for these conditions. The condition is likely related to shared lifestyle habits such as poor oral hygiene, tobacco or marijuana use, and coffee consumption. Hairy tongue is often referred to as black hairy tongue (lingua villosa nigra), but it may also appear in other colors such as brown, white, green, or pink, depending on secondary factors. The hairy areas are typically located on the posterior (back) part of the tongue and do not involve the underside of the tongue. Hairy tongue is not a harmful disorder and is usually asymptomatic. However, patients with hairy tongue may develop a secondary infection with Candida albicans (thrush). It remains unclear whether hairy tongue itself predisposes individuals to thrush, as the underlying causes of hairy tongue may also contribute to the development of thrush. Additionally, the use of Pepto-Bismol can cause the tongue and stool to turn black due to the formation of bismuth trisulfide (Bi₂S₃) when bismuth reacts with sulfur in saliva. The treatment for hairy tongue involves maintaining good oral hygiene and using a toothbrush or tongue scraper to aid in the desquamation of the tongue. Antifungal medications may be necessary if a candidal infection is suspected. If the condition is caused by antibiotic use, it may resolve naturally after the completion of the antibiotic course. In animals, black tongue is a condition observed in dogs, caused by a deficiency of niacin. This condition is associated with ulcers and inflammation of the oral cavity in affected dogs.
